brief: Marketing lead: changed one email subject line from feature-focused to outcome-focused; open rate up 31%; list of 18k subscribers.
original_draft:
We changed ONE email subject line — and open rates jumped 31%.

Here's the story.

For months, our emails to our 18k subscribers led with features: "New: Advanced Reporting Dashboard." Solid open rates. Nothing special.

Then we tried a simple experiment. Instead of describing the feature, we described the outcome — what the reader would actually get out of it.

Same email. Same list. Same send time. One change.

Open rate: up 31%. 📈

The lesson is as old as marketing itself, but clearly we needed the reminder: customers don't care about your features. They care about what your features do for them.

Feature-focused: "New: Advanced Reporting Dashboard"
Outcome-focused: "Find out where your pipeline is leaking"

One talks about you. The other talks about them.

Since then, we've rewritten every subject line in our lifecycle emails using the same principle — and the gains keep coming.

Marketers: audit your last 10 subject lines. How many talk about you vs your reader?

What's the best-performing subject line you've ever written? 👇

brief: Founder shares the 5 tools their 12-person team runs on: Linear, Notion, Slack, Figma, and a homegrown deploy bot named "Otto".
original_draft:
People often ask how our 12-person team stays productive without a big ops function.

The answer? We run the entire company on just 5 tools:

1️⃣ Linear — every task, bug, and project lives here. If it's not in Linear, it doesn't exist.
2️⃣ Notion — our company brain. Docs, wikis, meeting notes, onboarding.
3️⃣ Slack — communication, with strict channel hygiene to keep the noise down.
4️⃣ Figma — where every product idea becomes real before a single line of code is written.
5️⃣ Otto — our homegrown deploy bot. One command, and code goes from PR to production. Everyone's favorite teammate.

That's it. No sprawling tool stack. No overlapping subscriptions. No "wait, which doc is the source of truth?"

The principle behind it: every new tool adds a tax. Context-switching, licenses, onboarding, integrations. We only add a tool when the pain of not having it exceeds that tax.

Simplicity is a competitive advantage.

What tools could your team not live without? Drop your stack below. 👇

brief: Burnout post: took a 2-week sabbatical after 4 years without a real break; came back and killed 3 recurring meetings; advice about rest.
original_draft:
I just took my first real break in 4 years.

Two weeks. No Slack. No email. No "quick calls."

I'll be honest: the first few days were deeply uncomfortable. I checked my phone out of habit. I felt guilty. I convinced myself things would fall apart without me.

Spoiler: they didn't.

But the real insight came when I returned. With fresh eyes, I looked at my calendar and saw it clearly — so much of my busyness was self-inflicted. Within my first week back, I killed 3 recurring meetings that, it turns out, nobody missed.

Here's what burnout taught me:
🧠 Rest isn't a reward for finishing the work. The work is never finished.
🧠 If your business can't survive 2 weeks without you, that's a design flaw — not a badge of honor
🧠 Exhaustion is not a personality trait

To every founder and leader grinding without a break: the sabbatical you think you can't afford is probably the one you need most.

When was your last real break? Be honest. 👇

The useful part came after. I got back, looked at my calendar with two weeks of distance, and saw how much of my busyness was self-inflicted. I killed 3 recurring meetings in my first week back. Nobody has missed them.

Two things I believe now. Rest can't wait for the work to be finished, because the work is never finished. And if a business can't survive two weeks without its leader, that's a design flaw, not a badge of honor.

brief: Company milestone: hired employee #50; started 3 years ago with 4 people in a garage in Denver; now serving 900 customers.
facts: 4 people in a garage in Denver
original_draft:
3 years ago, we were 4 people in a garage in Denver.

This week, we welcomed employee #50. 🎉

I keep scrolling through old photos of that garage — the folding tables, the space heater, the whiteboard we bought off Craigslist — and honestly, I'm filled with gratitude.

Today, we serve 900 customers. But the numbers only tell part of the story.

What I'm most proud of isn't the growth. It's that the values we scribbled on that Craigslist whiteboard still guide how we operate every single day:
💛 Customers first, always
💛 Default to transparency
💛 Hire people better than yourself

To our first 4: thank you for believing when there was nothing to believe in.
To our newest 46: thank you for choosing us.
To our 900 customers: everything we do is for you.

Milestones like this are a moment to pause, reflect, and say thank you — before getting right back to work.

Here's to the next 50. 🚀

brief: Contrarian: networking events are mostly useless; the author got their last 3 clients from writing online, not conferences.
original_draft:
Unpopular opinion: networking events are mostly useless.

I used to attend every conference, every mixer, every "founder happy hour." I collected hundreds of business cards. Want to know how many clients came from all that networking?

Zero.

Meanwhile, my last 3 clients all came from the same place: writing online.

Here's why writing beats networking:

✍️ Scale — a conversation reaches one person; a post reaches thousands
✍️ Selection — the right people come to you, already pre-sold on how you think
✍️ Compounding — a good post keeps working for months; a handshake is forgotten by Monday

Networking events optimize for feeling productive. Writing optimizes for being findable.

Now, I'm not saying relationships don't matter — they're everything. But the best relationships start when someone reads your ideas and thinks, "this person gets it."

Stop collecting business cards. Start publishing your thinking.

Your next client isn't at a conference. They're scrolling their feed, waiting to discover you.

Agree? Or am I completely wrong? Let's debate. 👇

brief: Sharing a podcast appearance on "Supply Chain Weekly" about AI demand forecasting; episode 142; discussed forecast error down 18% at a pilot customer.

I had the pleasure of joining Supply Chain Weekly for episode 142 — and we went deep on one of my favorite topics: AI demand forecasting. 🎙️

We covered a lot of ground:
📦 Why traditional forecasting methods break down in volatile markets
🤖 What AI-driven forecasting actually looks like in practice (beyond the buzzwords)
📉 A real-world result: at one of our pilot customers, forecast error is down 18%

That last number is the one I keep coming back to. An 18% reduction in forecast error isn't an abstract metric — it means less overstock, fewer stockouts, and real working capital freed up.

We also got honest about the hard parts: data quality, change management, and why the forecasting team's expertise matters more with AI, not less.

A huge thank you to the hosts for the thoughtful questions and the great conversation.

brief: Year in review: ARR grew from $1.2M to $3.4M; team from 9 to 21; biggest mistake was hiring sales too early; NPS 61.
facts: biggest mistake was hiring sales too early
original_draft:
Our year in review — the numbers, the wins, and the mistake I'd take back.

📈 ARR: $1.2M → $3.4M
👥 Team: 9 → 21
💛 NPS: 61

By almost every measure, it was the best year in our company's history. But the metric I'm proudest of is that NPS — because growth means nothing if customers don't love what you build.

Now, the honest part. My biggest mistake this year: hiring sales too early.

We brought on sales reps before we, the founders, had truly nailed the sales motion ourselves. The result? Months of missed targets, frustrated reps, and expensive lessons. It wasn't their fault — it was mine. You can't hand off a playbook you haven't written.

We course-corrected, rebuilt the process from first principles, and things finally clicked. But I'd take those months back if I could.

I'm sharing this because year-in-review posts usually only show the highlight reel. Growth is messy.

Here's to the year ahead — and to learning in public. 🚀

What's your biggest lesson from this year? 👇

brief: VC newsletter segment on vertical SaaS; thesis: AI makes small vertical markets viable; example: software for marinas, a $400M TAM.
facts: Thesis: AI makes small vertical markets viable
original_draft:
This week, let's talk about vertical SaaS — and why we think the playbook is being rewritten in real time.

The old objection to vertical software was always market size. A niche industry might desperately need better tools, but if the TAM couldn't support a venture-scale outcome, investors passed. AI changes that math. When a small team can build, sell, and support software that previously required fifty people, small vertical markets suddenly become viable — and even attractive.

Take software for marinas: a $400M TAM that most funds would have ignored a decade ago. Today, an AI-native team can serve that market profitably at a fraction of the historical cost structure, own the core workflow end to end, and expand into payments, insurance, and adjacent services over time.

Our thesis is simple: the next generation of great vertical SaaS companies will be smaller teams attacking smaller markets — and capturing far more of them. If you're building in this space, we'd love to hear from you.
